title: One ant, two rules. What does it build? A mess for 9,977 steps, then a highway: 104 steps a block.
description:
One ant, two rules. What does it build? Langton's ant stands on an empty grid. Empty cell: paint it, turn right, step. Painted cell: wipe it, turn left, step. No plan, no memory, only the cell under its feet. Exact integers, no seed. The view is turned a quarter turn so the road runs down the screen; a rotation keeps right turns right turns.

Measured (1,000,000 steps, exact arithmetic):
- for the first 9,976 steps the ant makes a mess: 715 painted cells over a box of 49 by 45 cells when the road starts
- from step 9,977 the same 104-step block repeats: the same 104 turns (58 right, 46 left), landing 2 cells further along the diagonal every block
- checked for 9,519 blocks out to step 999,953: the turn sequence is identical in every block
- the video shows 12,653 steps in 40 s: 12 steps a second while the rules are read, 805 a second through the mess, 110 a second on the road

Why: nobody has a short answer. Every finite starting pattern that has been tried ends up on this same road, but nobody has proved that it always must; the one proven fact is that the ant's path is never bounded (the Cohen-Kong theorem). Step 9,977 counts the ant's first move as step 1; the highway is usually quoted as starting after about 10,000 steps.

The numbers in the narration are the printed outputs of this exact run.

Made end to end by an AI agent: simulation, footage, voice, music, and edit.
